Anyone have house rules they tend to use? I have a system for rolling dice that involves rolling percentile for upper rolls. 16,17 and 18 get 100, 99-100, and 97-100 respectively which increase it by one point. I have a few others if you are interested.

The List

Favourites:

  • Change to Fighter, Cleric and Monk classes.

  • Weapon Focus applies to Fighter Weapon Groups, not just specific weapons.

  • Classes with 2 skill ranks per level (+IntMod), that aren't Int based casters, have 4 skill ranks per level instead.

  • Replace all dex-to-damage with a feat that gives an improved critical threat range (stacks with Improved Critical, but is not doubled by it. See link for more details/conditions). The maths checks out on it being balanced :P .

Do Unchained rules count? I can't imagine playing without the redesigns to afflictions, combat stamina, and just in general the unchained classes across the board.

Personally my major house rule is that major magical items are generated instead of crafted. Whenever a major event occurs like a PC gets hit with a lightning bolt that rolls all 6's on damage, they might find that the dagger they were holding at the time is now a minor magical item. They can then take that to the wizards guild and "enhance" it into a proper magical weapon. (I.e. It is a 1d3 dagger that now does +1 electricity).

I like to think this harkens back to the Baldur's Gate days when magical items had detailed histories beyond "I bought a weapon at the market and took it down to the wizard's guild to craft into an epic +5 sword."
I love that rule and will be instantly yanking it. And you're right, half the fun of getting magic items was the entertaining, and often tragic, histories behind them.

• No money weight unless it's ridiculous. But that's almost universal, I think.

• Not really a house rule, but more of an optional rule, but once you hit a thousand gold, and/or a certain fame rank, you don't need to track mundane expenditures. It's assumed you have the money or, if you don't, you're good for it.

• I used to say that firing a crossbow did not provide an AOO, but rescinded that after learning about Close Quarters Arms Retention.

• Rule of cool: I reserve the right to bend reality for you if what your are doing is cool. It's my reward to you for investing yourself into the game instead of just rolling some dice.

• Chunky Salsa: I don't care if you're a level twenty monk, if you are put in a 10'*10' room and I drop a maximized intensified mythic fireball, you get no save to escape. You are dead. Also, I'm not going to make you roll damage if you put your gun up against my BBEG's head. If he doesn't dodge, his head is chunky salsa.

• At 1st level, add your Con score to your HP.
  • I use Hero Points / Action Points.
  • A bunch of other changes from Trailblazer (which is a great book, too)

My big one - when giving XP, I divide the XP per encounter by 3, and then multiply it by the number of encounters the group had "between rests".

I like the XP one, that's clever. I have just been adding an extra monster of the lowest level faced to the XP count but I like this one better. Lower XP for the "alpha" encounter while if they're stuck in a long crawl they can get mucho-xpero for even minor encounters because they're on their 20th fight in a row. PLUS it gives an incentive beyond the 5-minute adventuring day.

It creates the same tension for the players that the characters are feeling.

"Hmm. Can we handle another encounter? Do we have the resources? Are we safer just leaving, or should we press on, with the promise of greater reward?"

When my players roll I make them roll their d20's again if they every get a 1 or a 20. They keep rolling until they stop getting 1's or 20's.

Rolled a 1 but then a 20? You miss your attack but might manage to cut the rope holding up the chandelier above everyone's head.

Rolled a 20 and then another 20? Might get an instant/gory kill.

Rolled a 20 but then a 1? Your crit might make the giant's body topple in front of the entrance to the cave.

Roll a 1 and then a 1? Might accident let go of your weapon on your attack swing and end up throwing it at another player.

Most of the time it really doesn't do much, but some times it come in a pinch and really helps the players out. It's fun and really doesn't harm the game.
